query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduce a 2–3 atomic % aluminum addition into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to promote in situ formation of an adherent, protective Al2O3 scale without compromising the single-phase solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting good ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) but with poor oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Modify the base alloy composition by adding 2–3 at.% Al (yielding a target composition of, for example, HfNbTaTiZrAl with 2–3 at.% Al) followed by a thorough homogenization heat treatment to ensure chemical uniformity and avoid phase segregation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 800–1000 °C for a duration of 5 h, with subsequent tensile mechanical tests conducted at room temperature and at 1000 °C under quasi-static loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a thin, continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature exposure, while the bulk remains a single-phase solid solution.
generation.mechanism: The minor Al addition, due to its high oxygen affinity, preferentially oxidizes to form a stable, protective alumina layer. Thermodynamic calculations and CALPHAD analysis indicate that 2–3 at.% Al is sufficient to form the oxide without destabilizing the matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate, reduced mass gain, and the formation of an adherent Al2O3 scale, all while retaining its inherent ductility and yield strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which oxidizes rapidly under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The approach is effective only if the Al addition remains within 2–3 at.% and the homogenization prevents any undesirable phase formation; performance is limited to oxidizing environments up to ~1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: Although thermodynamic models support the formation of a protective Al2O3 scale, the long-term cyclic oxidation behavior and potential subtle effects on phase stability require further verification; however, recent analogous alloy studies validate this strategy.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two batches: the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy and the Al-modified alloy (with 2–3 at.% Al). Expose both to oxidation in air at 900 °C for 5 h, then perform surface analysis (SEM, XRD) and tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain response at both temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy fails to produce a continuous, well-adherent Al2O3 scale (e.g., shows similar oxidation or scale spallation) or if its mechanical properties are adversely affected relative to the base alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Next, we couple high-resolution electron microscopy, atom probe tomography, hybrid Monte-Carlo, special quasirandom structures, and density functional theory calculations to demonstrate how controlled additions of Al and Ti and subsequent annealing drive chemical ordering in nearly random equiatomic face-centered cubic CoFeNi solid solution. We establish that short-range ordered domains, the precursors of long-range ordered precipitates, inform mechanical properties. Specifically, a progressively increasing local order boosts the tensile yield strengths of the parent CoFeNi alloy by a factor of four while also substantially improving ductility, which breaks the so-called strength–ductility paradox. Finally, we validate the generality of our approach by predicting and demonstrating that controlled additions of Al, which has large negative enthalpies of mixing with the constituent elements of another nearly random body-centered cubic refractory NbTaTi HEA, also introduces chemical ordering and enhances mechanical properties.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. candidates.hypothesis: Apply a thin, dense alumina-based anti-oxidation coating with an optimized bond coat to the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to prevent high-temperature oxidation and pesting.
candidates.intervention: Deposit a thin (preferably 50–150 nm) alumina (Al2O3) coating using advanced methods such as magnetron sputtering or physical vapor deposition, preceded by a thin bond coat (e.g., a few nm of Ti or a graded interlayer) designed to accommodate thermal expansion differences.
candidates.changes: Expanded details on coating thickness, incorporation of a suitable bond/interlayer to mitigate thermal expansion mismatch, and discussion on process impacts. Added justification and referenced literature evidence from similar refractory/high‐entropy alloys.

candidates.hypothesis: Introduce a 2–3 atomic % aluminum addition into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to promote in situ formation of an adherent, protective Al2O3 scale without compromising the single-phase solid solution.
candidates.intervention: Modify the base alloy composition by adding 2–3 at.% Al (yielding a target composition of, for example, HfNbTaTiZrAl with 2–3 at.% Al) followed by a thorough homogenization heat treatment to ensure chemical uniformity and avoid phase segregation.
candidates.changes: Enhanced justification for the 2–3 at.% Al addition by referencing thermodynamic and CALPHAD-based studies, and included discussion on potential phase stability and the need for homogenization to avoid detrimental precipitates.

candidates.hypothesis: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to form a stable, adherent HfO₂-rich surface layer on the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy surface to a tailored pre-oxidation treatment by heating in an atmosphere with reduced oxygen partial pressure (≈0.1 atm O₂) at 750 °C for 2 h, with controlled ramp-up and ramp-down rates to minimize thermal shock.
candidates.changes: Added more explicit pre-oxidation process parameters, a discussion of potential competing oxides, and a recommendation for cyclic oxidation tests to check for spallation.

candidates.hypothesis: Perform a laser surface nitriding treatment on the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to form an ultrathin, uniform nitride layer (e.g., HfN/TiN rich) that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion and improves oxidation resistance without compromising bulk mechanical properties.
candidates.intervention: Apply a controlled laser surface nitriding process in a nitrogen-rich environment using optimized laser parameters (e.g., pulse duration, energy density) to induce rapid melting and re-solidification, forming a nanocrystalline nitride layer on the surface.
